title: Writeback Oscillation and Bank-Slant Exploratory Notes
content:
Goal:
Quickly capture an odd pattern we've been seeing in production and in repro lanes: periodic writeback/paging oscillations that spike NVMe qdepth and cause write stalls, coincident with large multi-request bursts. Hypothesis thread: alignment of resident-set fragments to memory-bank boundaries + writeback scheduling interacts poorly with our prefetch/pinning heuristics and causes a feedback loop that thrashes bandwidth and evicts hot KV pages.

Background / why this matters:
- Symptoms: short (200–900ms) latency spikes on long-context generations, p95->p99 jumps, NVMe write latency climbs, and downstream KV lookups hit more misses for ~1–3s after the spike.
- This isn't classic hot-key surge: traffic distribution is not skewed enough, and CPU/GPU are not saturated. Observed mainly on machines with 4-channel DIMM setups and NVMe tiers configured for async spillback.
- If repeatable it explains a nontrivial fraction of tail latency incidents under multi-tenant bursts.

Key observations so far (lab + prod traces):
1) Timeline correlation: writeback bursts precede KV miss-rate increase by ~50–200ms (writeback first, eviction/miss rate second).
2) Perf counters: DRAM channel utilization shows strong imbalance during spikes; one or two memory channels reach >85% while others idle ~30–40%.
3) NVMe: qdepth climbs to max configured depth, queue latency distribution becomes bimodal; bulk write completions delayed and group up, creating backpressure to page replacement code.
4) Hot page placements: resident-set fragmentation maps show that frequently used KV pages are co-located on a handful of physical pages that map to the same memory bank (likely due to allocator/placement + model weight layout).

Hypotheses (ranked):
A) Bank-slant + writeback scheduling: when dirty pages aligned to a small set of banks are flushed together, DMA engines saturate specific memory controllers and NVMe paths, causing writeback latency + reclaim stalling; eviction algorithm then selects more pages (because lower available residency), causing a cascade.
B) Prefetch/pinning interaction: our prefix KV pinning prevents early eviction but also creates larger contiguous ranges of dirty pages; when they become writeback-eligible they flush as a group.
C) Async spillback corner-case: under qdepth saturation the spillback queue defers some read-repopulate work which increases miss amplification for later requests.
D) Allocator placement bias: the memory allocator's slab sizing for KV pages ends up placing many entries on physical frames that share bank/channel mapping (particularly on our 8KB slab/4KB page boundary interplay).

Experiments run (lab):
- Synthetic replay: 5k concurrent chat sessions replayed to reproduce the spike on a 4-channel test node (setup: 4x16GB channels, NVMe x4). Repro rate ~70% when workload includes many long-context requests (~8k tokens) + bursts of short requests.
- Pin/unpin variant: toggled KV pinning heuristics (aggressive pin vs conservative). Aggressive pinning increased amplitude of writeback spikes but reduced immediate misses; conservative pinning reduced writeback peaks but increased short-term tail misses.
- Staggered writeback: forced jitter in writeback daemon (random 50–200ms jitter) smoothed NVMe qdepth spikes and lowered p99 by ~12% but increased avg latency by ~3ms. Indicates that batching of flushes contributes to tail.
- Channel striping: changed allocator to rotate placement across banks (simple round-robin at page allocation). This reduced single-channel saturation but increased overall DRAM activity; p99 improved in synthetic runs by ~18% but regression seen for some workloads that depend on locality.

Measurement artifacts / telemetry to add:
- Per-page physical frame -> bank/channel mapping (collect via /proc/pagemap + platform mapping utility) for traces where spikes occur.
- NVMe qdepth histograms per-second and per-io-queue.
- Writeback queue length and average batch size at time-of-flush.
- Resident-set fragmentation map: heatmap of logical key groups -> physical page frames.
- Memory controller stall counters per bank (iMC counters) and DMA engine stalls.

Actionable short-term mitigations (can ship quickly):
1) Add randomized jitter to writeback and prefetch queues (config flag) — low risk, empirically reduces simultaneous flushes.
2) Reduce aggressive pin window under high qdepth signals (adaptive pin shrink) — attempt to trade some immediate misses for lowered writeback amplitude.
3) Introduce a bank-aware allocator toggle: simple mode rotates allocations across banks; enable behind flag for high-tail incidents only.
4) Increase NVMe queue depth ceiling carefully or implement token-bucket on writeback to avoid queue saturation; must test impact on steady-state throughput.

Longer-term work / research tasks:
- Design eviction-aware allocator: allocate hot KV objects to interleaved set of banks with soft affinity to reduce correlated dirty-set flushes. Study effects on locality and cache-line spilling.
- Fine-grained writeback choreographer: build a scheduler that spaces flushes based on estimated physical bank spread (requires mapping or hints from allocator).
- Prefetch rewrite: make prefetch granularity adaptive to bank pressure signals and include backoff when NVMe qdepth high.
- Simulator: extend our bandwidth simulator to model bank-level saturation and writeback bursts (today it models aggregate bandwidth only).

Open questions / unknowns:
- How stable is bank mapping across reboots/cloud image variants? Does cloud hypervisor remap PFNs in ways that invalidate our physical placement assumptions?
- Are certain model families (dense embeddings vs decoder models) more vulnerable due to typical memory layout?
- Usability: how disruptive are allocation/placement changes to other parts of runtime (pools, CUDA pinned memory interaction)?
- Does increasing NVMe qdepth simply push latency later (worse tail), or absorb it safely? Needs stress testing.

Log / experiment snippets (commands & outputs):
- Collect per-page PFN -> bank mapping: sudo ./pfnbankmap /proc/kpageflags /proc/pagemap > pfn_bank.csv
- Quick qdepth trace (nvme-cli): sudo nvme monitor -o json > nvme-qtrace.json
- resident-set heatmap (toy script): python tools/rs_heatmap.py --trace replay-2024-11-12.trace --output heat.png

Mini playbook for on-call (how to triage when this shows up in prod):
1) Check NVMe qdepth and write latency for offending host (nvme stats + iostat -x).
2) Dump small resident-set sample and run pfnbankmap to see whether dirty pages are bank-clustered.
3) If cluster present, enable writeback-jitter flag and reduce pin window temporarily (feature flag rollout).
4) If intervention helps, schedule a ramped rollout of bank-rotating allocator for affected fleet subset.

Notes to self / follow-ups:
- Daniel to add a unit test in allocator that simulates bank-hot allocations and asserts distribution.
- Maria to prototype choreographer scheduler in a local branch for perf testing.
- Create a reproducible infra job that runs the synthetic multi-tenant burst every night for a week and collects full perf counters.

References / prior tickets: ENG-4523 (writeback spikes), SRE-788 (NVMe tail incidents), perf PR #998 (allocator changes), confluence:serving-runtime/paging-playbook.

Unresolved idea: map high-level key-group id -> physical bank hint at creation time and store in key metadata so eviction algorithm can purposefully scatter evictions when it notices bank clustering. Needs memory overhead analysis.

End-of-note: this doc intentionally informal. Goal is to capture the investigative thread and actionable mitigations to iterate rapidly.
